name: Primary central nervous system vasculitis
aliases: Primary angiitis of the central nervous system

reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
clinicalPearls: Primary CNS vasculitis is an inflammatory vasculopathy confined to the brain, spinal cord and leptomeninges, with no systemic vasculitis.
Presentation is typically insidious with headache and cognitive decline, punctuated by multifocal strokes or transient ischaemic events in different vascular territories.
Systemic inflammatory markers and ANCA are usually normal or negative, which helps distinguish it from systemic vasculitides.
Cerebrospinal fluid commonly shows a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and raised protein; a completely normal CSF makes the diagnosis much less likely.
Catheter angiography may show alternating stenosis and dilatation ('beading'), but is neither sensitive nor specific and can be normal in small-vessel disease.
Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy is the reference standard but has significant sampling error because the disease is patchy.
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is the key mimic and must be excluded before committing to prolonged immunosuppression.
High-resolution vessel-wall MRI showing concentric enhancement can support the diagnosis and help differentiate it from non-inflammatory vasculopathy.
reference.pathophysiology: Primary CNS vasculitis is characterised by inflammatory infiltration and destruction of the walls of small and medium arteries and veins restricted to the central nervous system. Histology varies from granulomatous inflammation (often with vascular amyloid deposition) to lymphocytic or acute necrotising patterns. The inflammation narrows and occludes vessels, producing ischaemia and infarction, and may weaken walls to cause haemorrhage. The stimulus is unknown and, by definition, there is no systemic vasculitic process; the disease is heterogeneous, affecting different calibre vessels in different patients, which accounts for its variable clinical and radiological picture.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary CNS involvement by systemic vasculitis or connective tissue disease
CNS infection (varicella zoster, tuberculosis, fungal, syphilitic arteritis)
Intravascular lymphoma or other neoplastic vasculopathy
Cerebral amyloid angiopathy with associated inflammation
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain with diffusion and gradient-echo or susceptibility sequences
High-resolution vessel-wall MRI to assess mural enhancement
Catheter cerebral angiography where medium-vessel disease is suspected
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis including cell count, protein, cytology and infection screen
Systemic vasculitis and autoimmune serology (ANCA, ANA, complement) to exclude secondary causes
Brain and leptomeningeal biopsy in selected cases
Screening for infective and neoplastic mimics including varicella zoster PCR
redFlags: Rapidly progressive encephalopathy or reduced consciousness
Spinal cord involvement with evolving myelopathy
New seizures with progressive cognitive decline
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease can progress to disabling stroke, cognitive impairment or death, but many patients respond to immunosuppression; the granulomatous and small-vessel subtypes may relapse and require prolonged therapy. Early diagnosis and exclusion of mimics substantially improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome as vasculitis and giving unnecessary long-term immunosuppression.
Relying on angiographic 'beading' as diagnostic when it is non-specific and often absent in small-vessel disease.
Excluding the diagnosis on a single negative biopsy given the patchy distribution of disease.
Overlooking infective arteritis, particularly varicella zoster, before starting immunosuppression.
Attributing an isolated stroke in a young patient to atherosclerosis without considering CNS vasculitis.
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology, current edition
Oxford Textbook of Medicine, current edition
Consensus reviews on primary angiitis of the central nervous system
management: Induce remission with high-dose corticosteroids combined with cyclophosphamide
Maintain remission with azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil once disease is controlled
Reserve rituximab for refractory or relapsing disease
Exclude mimics such as infection, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, and malignancy before immunosuppression
Track disease activity with serial MRI and clinical assessment to detect relapse
Provide prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia, osteoporosis, and gastric ulceration during immunosuppression
Manage within a neurology and rheumatology multidisciplinary team
